data.title: Galaxy: Observing Institutional Holdings of Bitcoin ETPs from 13F Data
data.description:
Author: Alex Thorn, Managing Director and Head of Research at Galaxy Digital; Translated by Shaw, Jinse Finance

Introduction

In the third quarter of 2026, institutions regained their position as net buyers of U.S. spot Bitcoin exchange-traded products (ETPs).

Investment managers who filed 13F holdings reports with the U.S. SEC made a net purchase equivalent to 49,229 Bitcoins. This is the largest net purchase since the second quarter of 2025, and it also exceeds the net sale of 47,054 Bitcoins in the previous three quarters combined.

As of September 30, 2026, the number of Bitcoins held by reporting institutions reached 356,491 (worth $29.78 billion), a record high. Half of this net increase in holdings came from investment advisors and wealth management platforms; both the number of Bitcoins and the proportion of these holdings in total institutional holdings reached their peak since the launch of Bitcoin ETPs in January 2024. During the third quarter (July 1 – September 30), a period of continuous accumulation, the Bitcoin price ranged from the bear market low of $57,717 on July 1 to the recent high of $87,397 on September 21. Note: This report only includes holders of US-based spot Bitcoin ETPs and does not include similar products issued overseas. Key Takeaways

  • Investment advisors and wealth management platforms have reached record highs across all metrics. This category includes Registered Investment Advisors (RIAs), wealth management institutions, large brokerages (Wirehouse), and brokerage trading platforms; as of September 30, 2026, its holdings were equivalent to 144,307 Bitcoins, accounting for 40.5% of the total 13F-reported spot Bitcoin ETP holdings and 11.2% of the total underlying Bitcoin holdings of all funds, both of which are the highest values ​​in this statistical series. This sector's holdings have increased for nine consecutive quarters, reaching 3.3 times the size on March 31, 2024; a decline only occurred once in the second quarter after its launch, namely the second quarter of 2024. This sector's share of total 13F holdings has risen for five consecutive quarters, from 22.2% on June 30, 2025, after declining for three consecutive quarters. They are also the most stable buyers. Investment advisors and wealth management platforms have been net buyers for nine consecutive quarters; from Q2 2024 to Q3 2026, all reporting institutions increased their holdings by a total of 179,300 Bitcoins, of which 100,003 were contributed by this sector. In the three quarters ending June 30, 2026, when institutions were net sellers overall, this sector still increased its holdings by 32,706 Bitcoins, while basis and relative value hedge funds sold 54,683 Bitcoins. The increase this quarter was mainly driven by large brokerages. This sector added a total of 24,838 bitcoins this quarter, of which 22,728 came from large brokerage and trading platforms, primarily Wells Fargo (+14,636 bitcoins), Bank of America (+7,201 bitcoins), and Morgan Stanley (+2,875 bitcoins). Breaking it down by business unit: Brokerage advisory and brokerage holdings increased from 30,978 bitcoins to 43,583 bitcoins, while trading and market-making holdings increased from 3,982 bitcoins to 12,551 bitcoins, with the majority of the increase coming from Bank of America. Wells Fargo became the largest holder in the 13F reporting system for the first time. Its declared holdings amounted to 30,553 bitcoins (worth $2.55 billion), nearly doubling from 15,931 bitcoins on June 30, 2026, surpassing Jane Street, which ranked first in the previous quarter. No wealth management platform had previously topped the list: Millennium Management had been the largest holder from Q1 2024 to Q1 2026. The breadth of participation in holdings has recovered, but net increases are concentrated in a few leading institutions. The number of managers holding spot Bitcoin funds increased by 191 to 2,166, ending two consecutive quarters of decline: 358 institutions that had no holdings in the previous quarter added new positions, while 167 institutions liquidated their positions. The newly entered institutions have relatively small holdings, totaling only 9,554 bitcoins. The top 50 holding institutions net increased their holdings by 59,578 coins; all other managers (including those exiting the market) net sold a total of 10,349 coins.

  • 13F reporting institutions hold 27.6% of the underlying Bitcoin in ETP. This percentage is higher than 24.8% on June 30, 2026, and slightly lower than the historical high of 27.7% on December 31, 2024. The remaining 72.4% is held by investors who are not required to file 13F reports, including individual investors, advisors who do not meet the reporting threshold, and the vast majority of overseas investors.

  • Hedge fund holdings account for less than 20%, a significant drop from the previous 50%. The three types of hedge funds collectively accounted for 19.0% of the total 13F reported holdings, compared to 50.6% on December 31, 2024. Basis and relative value funds held a total of 34,053 Bitcoins, a significant decrease from the peak of 101,826 Bitcoins on December 31, 2024; however, both these funds and macro funds were net buyers this quarter (adding 9,184 and 10,492 Bitcoins respectively). BlackRock's IBIT accounts for two-thirds of total institutional holdings. Reporting institutions collectively held the equivalent of 232,453 Bitcoins in IBIT, representing 65.2% of their total reported holdings; of the total net increase of 49,229 Bitcoins this quarter, IBIT contributed 34,744 Bitcoins. Institutional holdings of GBTC declined for the tenth consecutive quarter, with Grayscale Bitcoin Mini Trust's holdings surpassing GBTC for the first time. The vast majority of reported holders are US-based institutions. US-managed holdings reached a new high of 293,830 Bitcoins, accounting for 82.5% of the total 13F reported holdings; the proportion of holdings by foreign managers decreased from 18.6% to 17.5% (the peak was 24.0% on September 30, 2025). Although foreign managers' holdings increased from 57,274 to 62,456 Bitcoins, the increase in holdings by US-based institutions was greater, thus passively reducing the proportion.

  • Limitations of 13F Data: 13F only discloses long positions at the end of the quarter and only counts accounts where the manager has investment decision-making power. Short positions and most derivatives are not included in the reporting scope; ETP shares held by market makers and basis funds may be accompanied by hedging operations. Client-mandated brokerage accounts are generally not included in the statistics, therefore the actual holdings of wealth management channels may be underestimated. Furthermore, this data is only a snapshot as of September 30, 2026. As of November 16, 2026, the underlying Bitcoin holdings of the relevant funds have decreased by 38,531 coins, down to 1,252,139 coins.

Q3 2026 Data Overview

As of September 30, 2026, a total of 2,166 managers declared holdings in 13 spot Bitcoin funds, equivalent to 356,491 Bitcoins (US$29.78 billion). The number of managers increased by 191 from June 30. Excluding Bitcoin price fluctuations and based on shareholding, the net increase in institutional holdings this quarter was equivalent to 49,229 Bitcoins, approximately US$4.11 billion at the end of the quarter. 358 institutions opened new positions this quarter, 167 liquidated their positions, and 1,808 institutions held positions for two consecutive quarters.

Largest Institution in Net Increase

  • Wells Fargo: +14,636, from 15,931 to 30,553

  • Brevan Howard: +8,606, from 4,082 to 12,686

  • Brevan Howard: +8,606, from 4,082 to 12,686

  • Bank of America: +7201, from 1225 to 8424. Millennium Management: +7114, from 7417 to 14516. Jane Street: +6180, from 17007 to 23167. Largest net seller: Walleye Capital: −3270, from 3642 to 370. Galaxy Digital: -2721, down from 7519 to 4786. Avenir Tech: -2274, down from 7675 to 5396. Cantor Fitzgerald: -1680, down from 3650 to 1949. Bank of Montreal: -1632, down from 2648 to 1014. Largest new holdings. Balyasny Asset Management: 1782 Bitcoins D. E. Shaw: 1075 Bitcoins E. SigFig Wealth Management: 884 Bitcoins F. Garda Capital Partners: 625 Bitcoins G. Symmetry Investments: 423 Bitcoins All figures are converted to Bitcoin (see the methodology section for calculation details). Data is as of November 17, 2026 (one day after the filing deadline), with a total of 2166 13F filings collected. In previous quarters, only 97.7% of the documents were submitted by the deadline. Subsequent late submissions and revisions may still change this figure.

    Institutional Holdings

    This section's charts show the size of institutional holdings: the proportion of institutional holdings to the total underlying Bitcoin of the fund, the number of portfolio managers, and the distribution of holdings by Bitcoin quantity, USD amount, and percentage per fund.

    Spot Bitcoin ETP Holdings by 13F Filing Entities

    As of September 30, 2026, spot Bitcoin ETPs held a total of 1,290,670 Bitcoins, with a market value of $107.81 billion.

    The managers who submitted 13F filings reported holdings of 356,286 Bitcoins, accounting for 27.6%, higher than 24.8% on June 30, but slightly lower than the historical high of 27.7% on December 31, 2024. The remaining 72.4% (934,383 Bitcoins) were held by investors who were not required to submit 13F filings, including individual investors, investment advisors who did not meet the reporting threshold, and the vast majority of overseas investors. The top ten reporting institutions held a total of 149,388 Bitcoins, accounting for 11.6% of the total ETP Bitcoin supply and 41.9% of the total holdings of reporting institutions. This concentration reached 59.4% on March 31, 2024, and fell to a low of 34.2% on March 31, 2026; large-scale purchases by multiple institutions this quarter pushed up the concentration. The remaining 2,154 reporting institutions held a total of 206,898 Bitcoins (representing 16.0% of all ETP Bitcoins). This snapshot of the reporting data corresponds to September 30, 2026, and since then, the relevant funds have experienced continuous net outflows. The dotted line shows that as of November 16, 2026, the underlying Bitcoin holdings of the funds decreased to 1,252,139, a reduction of 38,531 from the end of the quarter; during the same period, the price of Bitcoin fell from $83,580 to $64,943. The trading activities of these institutions during this period of decline will only be known after the next round of 13F disclosures in February of the following year. The number of managers holding at least one spot Bitcoin ETP increased by 191 to 2,166, ending two consecutive quarters of decline and marking the first rebound. This number is more than double that of the end of the first quarter after the fund's launch (March 31, 2024, when there were 1009 institutions), and is still 85 institutions short of the historical peak of 2251 institutions on December 31, 2025. BlackRock's IBIT has the broadest institutional coverage, with 1648 managers holding it, accounting for 76% of all reporting institutions, 35 fewer than its own peak. Following closely are GBTC (677 institutions), FBTC (665 institutions), Grayscale Bitcoin Mini Trust (511 institutions), and BITB (310 institutions); HODL's number of holding institutions reached 138, a new high. Most institutions have relatively small holdings. Of the 2,166 managers, half held the equivalent of less than 10.4 Bitcoins (equivalent to approximately $870,000 at the quarter-end price), and another 215 held less than 1 Bitcoin. Therefore, the number of managers reflects the prevalence of this type of fund, rather than the total size of institutional Bitcoin holdings.

    Bitcoin holdings of 13F reporting institutions corresponding to each ETP

    The total holdings of reporting institutions in various spot Bitcoin funds are equivalent to 356,491 Bitcoins, a record high, exceeding the previous record of 354,299 Bitcoins on September 30, 2025 by 2,192 Bitcoins. Compared to 175,588 Bitcoins on March 31, 2024, the holding size has nearly doubled.

    New and Exiting 13F Holding Institutions

    The next chart breaks down changes in the number of managers into two categories: new entrants and exits. In the third quarter of 2026, 358 managers had no positions in the previous quarter but opened new positions in this quarter; 167 managers held positions in the previous quarter but liquidated them in this quarter; and 1808 managers held positions for two consecutive quarters, resulting in a net increase of 191 managers.

    Top Holding Institutions

    Investment managers' holdings in Bitcoin ETP are highly concentrated. The top ten institutions by reported size account for 42.0% of all reported holdings, the top 25 account for 60.8%, and the top 50 account for 71.2%. Therefore, a few institutions dominate the changes in holdings each quarter.

    Top 13F Holders of US Spot Bitcoin ETPs

    Wells Fargo is the largest holder of spot Bitcoin ETPs according to 13F filings, with a total of 30,553 Bitcoins held across 10 funds, worth $2.55 billion. This represents a significant increase from 15,931 Bitcoins as of June 30, 2026, surpassing Jane Street (23,167 Bitcoins) which previously held the top spot. Millennium Management ranks fourth with 14,516 Bitcoins; it had consistently held the top position for several quarters from Q1 2024 to Q1 2026.

    Top 13F Holders of US Spot Bitcoin ETPs

    The top 15 holding institutions cover a wide range of entities in the institutional market: 3 wealth management platforms (Wells Fargo, Morgan Stanley, Bank of America), 5 market makers or bank trading desks (Jane Street, Goldman Sachs, Marex, Susquehanna, JPMorgan Chase), 3 hedge funds (Millennium Management, Brevin Howard, Schonfeld), 2 asset management companies (Horizon Kinetics, BlackRock), 1 sovereign wealth fund (Mubadala Investment Company), and 1 family office/corporate holding entity (Avenir Tech). Understanding this holding structure is crucial: the same amount of ETP shares might be client allocation positions on wealth management platforms, inventory in the hands of market makers, and one end of a hedging transaction in hedge funds; the same bank might also include all three types of positions in a single filing.

    Top 25 Holding Institutions and Their Quarterly Changes

    The top 25 holding institutions reported holdings equivalent to 216,629 Bitcoins, accounting for 60.8% of the total reported holdings. Among these 25 institutions, 17 increased their holdings, 6 decreased their holdings, and 2 maintained their holdings. Their combined net increase was 56,922 Bitcoins, higher than the total net increase of 49,229 Bitcoins from all 2,166 reporting institutions.

    Top 50 Holding Institutions and Their Quarterly Net Changes

    The next chart expands the statistical scope to the top 50 holding institutions, whose combined holdings account for 71.2% of the total reported holdings. The chart only shows changes in holdings. Among these 50 institutions, 30 increased their holdings, 15 decreased their holdings, and 5 maintained their holdings, resulting in a net increase of 59,578 Bitcoins.

    Holding Entity Classification

    This section's charts categorize all reporting institutions into eight major holding types, tracking the holding size and fund flows of each type. The key highlights for this quarter are here. Investment advisors and wealth platforms (including Registered Investment Advisors (RIAs), wealth management institutions, large integrated securities firms, and brokerage trading platforms) are the leading holding entities by size and have been the most stable buyers since the launch of Bitcoin ETP.

    Quarterly Bitcoin Holdings by Holding Entity Type

    As of September 30, 2026, investment advisors and wealth management platforms reported holdings equivalent to 144,307 Bitcoins, a new high since statistics began, 3.3 times the 44,053 Bitcoins held on March 31, 2024.

    Percentage of each type of holding entity in 13F reported holdings

    The next chart converts the above holding data into percentage form, making it easier to observe changes in the holding structure. Investment advisors and wealth management platforms account for 40.5% of the total spot Bitcoin ETP holdings reported in 13F, a record high since statistics began; the percentage was 24.3% in the same period last year and 25.1% on March 31, 2024. This percentage has been rising for five consecutive quarters since June 30, 2025, when it reached 22.2%. Prior to this, the increase was not sequential: the percentage declined in Q2 2024 due to selling by large securities firms; it fell again in Q4 2024 and Q2 2025 – during these periods, investment advisors continued buying, but hedge funds and trading institutions were more aggressive in their purchases. If we use all Bitcoin held by ETP funds (including those not held by 13F reporting entities) as the denominator, this category accounts for 11.2%, up from 5.3% on March 31, 2024, and has seen nine consecutive quarters of growth. The combined percentage of the three types of hedge funds is 19.0%, a significant drop from the peak of 50.6% on December 31, 2024. Of these, basis and relative value strategy funds alone saw their share shrink from 33.9% on March 31, 2024, to 9.6%. The share of market makers and bank trading desks remained stable between 16.8% and 23.7% for a long time, reaching 21.8% at the end of this quarter. The next chart separately shows the data for the third quarter of 2026. Of the eight major holders, five categories increased their holdings while three categories decreased them. Among the 12 listed products, all reporting institutions collectively increased their holdings by a net 49,176 tokens, with investment advisors and wealth management platforms contributing 24,838 tokens, accounting for 50.5% of the increase; followed by market makers and bank trading desks (+14,600 tokens), macro hedge funds (+10,492 tokens), and basis and relative value hedge funds (+9,184 tokens). Pension funds, sovereign wealth funds, and endowment funds maintained relatively stable holdings (+181 tokens). The entities that decreased their holdings were other hedge funds and crypto institutions (-5,295 tokens), family offices and corporate entities (-3,798 tokens), and asset management companies (-1,024 tokens). Family offices and corporate entities have decreased their holdings for three consecutive quarters; asset management companies saw their first net decrease during the statistical period. Regarding the largest increase in the bar, one additional point should be made: the investment advisor category includes large, integrated brokerage firms. Internal breakdowns within these firms show that their trading brokerage divisions' holdings of Bitcoin increased from 3,982 to 12,551 this quarter. The trading behavior of these divisions is more similar to that of market makers and bank trading desks, as shown in the second item of the chart.

    Quarterly Net Changes in Holdings by Entity Type (Converted to Bitcoin)

    The table below shows the detailed data corresponding to the above holding entity chart, and further breaks down some entity types. Three major trends are worth noting.

    First, within investment advisors and wealth management platforms, the main buyers have shifted from independent institutions to large platforms.

    Registered Investment Advisors (RIAs) and wealth managers increased their holdings in 9 out of 10 quarters, contributing 51,567 of the 100,003 new holdings in this category; however, the inflow of funds has narrowed significantly since 2026 (+2,492, -1,565, +2,110). Large integrated securities firms and brokerage trading platforms have increased their holdings for nine consecutive quarters, with the growth rate continuing to rise: 3,998 new holdings in Q1 2026, 11,953 in Q2, and 22,728 in Q3. Secondly, basis and relative value strategy hedge funds are the only category with a negative cumulative net increase (-25,365 new holdings). Since March 31, 2024, their selling volume has exceeded their buying volume. Third, sovereign wealth funds and government entities increased their holdings by a total of 13,142 tokens from the fourth quarter of 2024 to the first quarter of 2026, and have never experienced a net reduction in holdings during any quarter. Their current holdings are 13,101 tokens. Large integrated securities firms and brokerage trading platforms: Holding positions divided by business unit. When submitting Form 13F, banks or securities firms often consolidate multiple subsidiaries in their filings. Therefore, a large brokerage's total holdings include both client accounts under its wealth advisory division and proprietary positions on its trading desk. This table breaks down positions by business segment based on the list of managers specified in each filing. The 19 institutions in this group collectively hold the equivalent of 63,858 Bitcoins (worth $5.34 billion), up from 41,202 on June 30, 2026. Of these, the wealth advisory and brokerage division holds 43,583 Bitcoins, the trading brokerage division holds 12,551, the banking and trust division holds 5,256, and the asset management and other divisions hold 2,468. The wealth advisory and brokerage division's holdings increased by 41% this quarter from 30,978, confirming the core conclusion: the wealth management channel itself is still increasing its holdings. However, the holdings of the trading brokerage department increased from 3,982 to 12,551, more than doubling; the advisory department's share in this group decreased from 75.2% to 68.2%. If only Registered Investment Advisors (RIAs) and the aforementioned brokerage advisory departments are considered, the total holdings through the wealth management channel amount to 124,032 Bitcoins, higher than the previous 109,548, setting a new historical high for this metric; however, its share of all 13F-reported holdings slightly decreased from 35.6% to 34.8%. These three institutions account for 83.5% of the total holdings in this group. Wells Fargo holds a total of 30,553 Bitcoins, of which 85.1% is in the wealth advisory and brokerage department (26,016 Bitcoins, previously 13,219). Morgan Stanley's 14,354 holdings are spread across its advisory division (7,141), trading brokerage division (4,925), and asset management and other divisions (2,288). Bank of America is an exception: of its 8,424 holdings, 7,626 belong to its trading brokerage division (previously only 421), and only 16 to its advisory division. We believe Bank of America's increase comes from its trading portfolio, rather than from wealth management client demand. The 13F report only counts assets for which the manager has independent investment decision-making power. Client-directed brokerage accounts are typically not included in this data, therefore this statistic underestimates the actual size of institutional clients' holdings.

    Geographical Distribution of Holding Institutions

    Subsequent charts are compiled according to the main office location of each manager. Multinational banks or large integrated securities firms are categorized by their headquarters location; therefore, this map reflects the manager's registered location, not the location of their clients. Furthermore, managers outside the United States are only required to file a 13F report if they manage at least $100 million in U.S. equity securities; therefore, the data for foreign institutions represents the lower limit.

    Managers headquartered in the United States held a total of 293,830 Bitcoins, accounting for 82.5% of the total 13F reported holdings, the highest value during the statistical period. 111 overseas managers held a total of 62,456 Bitcoins, accounting for 17.5%.

    The United Kingdom and Crown Dependencies are the largest region outside the United States, holding 25,550 Bitcoins, higher than the 16,699 Bitcoins on June 30, 2026, but only about half of the peak of 50,138 Bitcoins on September 30, 2025. The Asia-Pacific region held 14,938 Bitcoins, declining for three consecutive quarters since its peak of 24,353 Bitcoins.

    The Middle East saw a record high of 14,525 contracts held, making it the only region to consistently increase its holdings over the past eight quarters. Canada (2,633 contracts), offshore financial centers (2,520 contracts), Europe outside the UK (2,000 contracts), and Latin America (290 contracts) all had smaller holdings.

    Quarterly Net Increase by Manager Geography

    In the third quarter of 2026, US managers made a net increase of 43,961 Bitcoins, the highest single-quarter increase since the fourth quarter of 2024, accounting for 89% of the total increase for the quarter.

    The UK and Crown Dependencies increased their holdings by 8,850 Bitcoins this quarter, marking the first net increase after three consecutive quarters of total reductions of 33,338 Bitcoins.

    This shift primarily stemmed from one institution: Brevin Howard, registered in Jersey, which increased its holdings by 8,606 tokens. The Middle East added 360 tokens, extending its record of net purchases to eight consecutive quarters. The Asia-Pacific region (-2,109 tokens) and Canada (-1,746 tokens) saw the largest reductions, with the Asia-Pacific region having been a net seller for three consecutive quarters. The chart also shows that the selling activity rotated between different regions from the end of 2025 to the beginning of 2026. In the fourth quarter of 2025, the UK and Crown Dependencies reduced their holdings by 20,206 tokens, while the Asia-Pacific region increased its holdings by 7,136 tokens. In the first quarter of 2026, US institutions reduced their holdings by 23,515 tokens. By the second quarter of 2026, the US had turned to buying (+13,494 tokens), but the UK and Crown Dependencies and the Asia-Pacific region continued to reduce their holdings.

    Foreign Holdings by Country/Region

    The four jurisdictions together account for 76% of the reported Bitcoin holdings by foreign managers. The UAE ranks first with the equivalent of 13,842 Bitcoins (accounting for 22.2% of total foreign holdings), almost entirely held by two sovereign wealth funds in Abu Dhabi. Jersey ranks second with 13,149 Bitcoins, more than doubling its holdings this quarter from 4,121 Bitcoins, mainly due to increased holdings by Brevin Howard, who is registered there. The UK (12,399 tokens) remained largely unchanged. Hong Kong (8,348 tokens) saw a decrease of about one-third from 12,408 tokens, due to reductions in holdings by Avenir Tech and Laurore. Following closely behind were Australia (3,127 tokens), Singapore (2,997 tokens), Canada (2,633 tokens), and the Cayman Islands (2,219 tokens). Canada had the largest number of applicants outside the US (27), but the individual holdings were relatively small. Continental Europe generally had lower reported holdings, with Italy (735 tokens) and Switzerland (689 tokens) ranking relatively high.

    US 13F Holdings: By State

    In the United States, New York State holds a dominant position. Local managers hold the equivalent of 138,825 Bitcoins, representing 47.2% of total US holdings and 39.0% of all 13F reported holdings. Many leading hedge funds, market makers, banks, and asset management institutions are based there.

data.title: Anthropic goes public; the first super-intelligent stock surges on opening.
data.description:
Last night, the largest IPO in history officially rang the bell!

This time, Anthropic truly made history, after opening,soaring all the way to $2 trillion.

At 00:48 Beijing time on November 20, Anthropic (NASDAQ: ANT) finally completed its first transaction since its listing.

At 00:48 Beijing time on November 20, Anthropic (NASDAQ: ANT) finally completed its first transaction since its listing.

The opening price was $111.50 per share, a surge of 34.3% over the offering price of $83, and a 59.3% higher than the lower end of the IPO roadshow pricing range of $70. With just this one transaction at the opening bell, the market was instantly flooded with buy orders for 140 million shares. Based on approximately 18.2 billion fully diluted shares, the market value would immediately exceed $2.03 trillion. Even if we only consider the approximately 13.2 billion outstanding shares, the value would still reach $1.47 trillion. Its market capitalization surpassed that of giants like Meta and Broadcom, ranking sixth among global listed companies! However, after an initial surge at the open, the stock price retreated somewhat. The intraday high reached $115.10, while the low was $92.72. At 5:00 AM Beijing time, the closing price was $97.17, still 17.1% higher than the offering price. [Image of a stock breaking 2 trillion yuan on its first day of trading, rewriting 400 years of IPO history] A company just over five years old entered the top six globally on its first day of trading, with a market capitalization exceeding 2 trillion yuan. What does $2 trillion mean? Since the first IPO in 1602, in over 400 years, no global stock market had ever reached the $2 trillion mark on its first day of trading. Before this, the title of the world's largest IPO was held by Elon Musk's SpaceX. At this moment, the record was rewritten. Anthropic's public offering raised a staggering $81.34 billion, surpassing SpaceX's $75 billion, with its shares surging 34.3% at the open and reaching a high of 38.5% during the day. This surge has left SpaceX far behind. In the 400-year history of the stock market, two of the three largest IPOs are scheduled for 2026. A pure-play, cutting-edge AI lab has taken the top spot for the first time. Looking back a year, Anthropic's wealth ballooned at an even more astonishing rate. Last September, Anthropic's valuation after a funding round was $183 billion. In 14 months, its value has skyrocketed by a full 11 times. Looking at global stock markets, only five tech companies remain ahead of it: Apple, Microsoft, Nvidia, Google, and Amazon. Its market capitalization surged past $2 trillion, triggering the most massive wave of wealth creation in Silicon Valley history. Overnight, Anthropic created 5,300 millionaires, with an average net worth exceeding $100 million. In the history of human commerce, no company has ever been able to propel thousands of ordinary employees to the pinnacle of wealth in just five years. Based on the offering price of $83 per share, the total value of the stock held by these 5,300 employees is a staggering $232 billion. On average, each person is worth $44 million, equivalent to 310 million RMB. If we include the initial surge to $111.50 at the open, this figure has already soared to over $58 million, or more than 400 million RMB! Of course, this enormous fortune is not distributed equally. Because a large number of employees are newcomers who joined in the last two years, the early employees have reaped the most dramatic benefits. An internal investor at Anthropic revealed that at least 400 early employees have a net worth exceeding $100 million, equivalent to over $700 million. Even more remarkably, several ordinary early employees who were not founders may have a net worth exceeding $1 billion, directly joining the billionaire club. As for the seven co-founders who left OpenAI, they were not included in the aforementioned "employee pool." Each of the seven founders held 230 million to 240 million shares, and based on the opening price of $111.50, their individual net worth was approaching $26 billion. These idealists who rented an office in San Francisco to write code back then became regulars on the global rich list five years later.

The world's seven giants stood in a row,A massive order for 900.9 billion computing power flowed back to the market

On Thursday morning, the air at Nasdaq was thick with the smell of burning US dollars.

Wall Street institutions were scrambling, with global institutional subscription demand reaching $500 billion, an oversubscription of more than 6 times.

Wall Street institutions were red-eyed, with global institutional subscription demand reaching $500 billion, an oversubscription of more than 6 times.

The most heated discussion online right now revolves around Anthropic's almost surreal shareholder list. These tech giants, usually locked in fierce competition, are all sitting side-by-side tonight, supporting Anthropic. The seven giants that have invested are Microsoft, Nvidia, TSMC, Micron, AMD, Broadcom, and Google. Each pair on this list is full of dramatic contrasts. Microsoft has OpenAI behind it, Google has its own Gemini, and Nvidia and AMD have been fiercely competing for over a decade, yet this time they've both bought shares in the same company. The secret to bringing these seven arch-rivals together lies in a single line of numbers on page 174 of the prospectus. Prior to its IPO, Anthropic had signed approximately $900.9 billion in procurement and leasing commitments, almost entirely spent on computing power and infrastructure, with commitments extending as far as 2045. In short, this is a top-tier "computing power internal circulation" in Silicon Valley. Giants joined forces to prop up Anthropic, drawing $81.34 billion from the public market and adding $26 billion in private placements, injecting a massive $107.3 billion in cash into the company. However, after receiving this record-breaking "AI arms deal," Anthropic had to spend it all. Purchasing Nvidia and AMD chips, customizing Broadcom ASICs, securing advanced wafer capacity from TSMC, and buying Micron's HBM high-bandwidth memory on a massive scale, plus paying exorbitant cloud computing power rental fees to Amazon, Google, and Microsoft—all this money, moving from one hand to the other, ultimately flows back into the pockets of these shareholders. Now, these giants who sell shovels are both shareholders of Claude and the computing power foundation beneath Claude's feet. After the bell rang, Ultraman couldn't sleep. Amidst this massive fundraising frenzy, the most awkward position belongs to its old rival, OpenAI. Anthropic raised over $100 billion in just one morning, leaving OpenAI completely stunned. The person who can't sleep the most tonight is definitely Ultraman! Previously, Altman had firmly adhered to his psychological bottom line of a "$1 trillion valuation." Now, his former subordinate has pushed the IPO valuation ceiling to $2 trillion. The global capital market's liquidity pool for pursuing cutting-edge big models is ultimately finite. As a result, industry insiders have reported that OpenAI has been forced to postpone its IPO plans to 2027, and the scale of its new round of private equity financing is also facing reduction.

What Wall Street bought was AI writing its own code

Faced with a staggering market capitalization of $2 trillion, Wall Street is not without its cold scrutiny.

After all, according to traditional financial valuation models, a company that is still losing money could never support a market value of $2 trillion.

After all, according to traditional financial valuation models, a company that is still losing money could never support a market value of $2 trillion.

Anthropic continues to incur losses. In the first three quarters of this year, Anthropic's total revenue was $33.2 billion, with an operating loss of $1.26 billion. For every $1 in revenue, $0.57 is burned through computing power and infrastructure. In the same period last year, this figure was $1.72. Someone once calculated that, based on a long-term computing power contract worth $900.9 billion, Anthropic would have to earn more in the next year than Google or Apple's total annual revenue to justify this astronomical investment. The market's willingness to pay this price was entirely driven by another sentence in the prospectus—"As of September 2026, over 90% of the code newly added to the Anthropic codebase will be written by Claude himself." METR's on-site audit also confirms this flywheel effect. Anthropic's AI development schedule, which originally took two years to complete, has been compressed to within one year, with 80% of that being attributed to AI. As trading resumed tonight, rumors began circulating in Silicon Valley that Anthropic would soon unveil its next-generation flagship models, Opus 5.6 and Fable 5.5. Wall Street's yardstick for pricing tech companies has completely changed tonight. Traditional stock pricing relies on the profit and loss statement to determine how much money a company is currently making. Tonight's $2 trillion price tag, however, is the first time Wall Street has offered a price based on the "self-evolving speed of its models." In the official listing address released tonight, Dario Amodei, in the second sentence, expressed the deep-seated aspirations he and his sister Daniela shared. He said, "My father and Daniela's father died of a disease, and just a few years later, a cure became available." They hope that in the future, fewer families will miss out on a cure by just a few years. Starting at 00:48 Beijing time tonight, every second the numbers on global stock markets are publicly quoting prices for the timeline to superintelligence. $2 trillion is just the first price offered today. Every subsequent rise and fall will depend on how much shorter Claude can shorten those years of waiting that humanity has been enduring.

data.title: What will become of Jensen Huang and Nvidia in the future?
data.description:
Author: Li Nannan

Over the past week, news about Jensen Huang has continued to dominate trending topics. We talked about Jensen Huang and the short drama industry some time ago, and just a couple of days ago, an AI short drama about Jensen Huang appeared on Douyin. You can get a sense of how far this whole thing has gone.

Currently, there are three key milestones in this matter. The first milestone is that Nvidia officially approved Jensen Huang's resignation. The second milestone is that Nvidia employees and the tech industry jointly voiced their support for Jensen Huang, and Jensen Huang himself also stated that he would be willing to return to Nvidia if needed. The third milestone is that Nvidia publicly stated that it is not currently considering bringing Jensen Huang back.

In a media interview, Musk said that Nvidia letting Jensen Huang go is equivalent to the Chicago Bulls firing Michael Jordan midway through a winning season. Online discussions about this generally focus on two questions: First, what will happen to Jensen Huang without Nvidia? Second, what will happen to Nvidia without Jensen Huang? What happens to companies that leave their founders afterward? Obviously, we can't directly predict the future, but we can find a frame of reference to see what happened to companies and founders who encountered similar situations in history. What kind of companies continue to thrive after their founders leave? What kind of founders remain sharp and insightful after leaving their companies? First, our selection criteria are limited to cases where the founder "suddenly left." Cases with smooth transitions following normal handover procedures are not considered. Second, these cases come from different industries, and their experiences may not be directly applicable to Jensen Huang and Nvidia. However, looking at them together, some commonalities may offer valuable insights. Let's answer the first question: What happened to the companies after the founder left? First, many of the founder's intuitions are indeed difficult to replace. For example, the most typical example is Sony. On November 30, 1993, Sony co-founder Akio Morita suffered a sudden brain hemorrhage while playing tennis. He survived, but was paralyzed on one side and never regained his ability to work. At that time, Sony was at its peak; it had just acquired Columbia Pictures four years earlier, the PS was in its final stages of development and ready for release, and the Walkman still dominated the global portable music player market. But Morita was the kind of person who would "make a strategy on a whim." The Walkman was his decision-making process; all market research indicated no one would wear headphones on the street, but he said, "I don't care, I'm going to do it," and it sold 400 million units. After Morita left, Sony almost completely collapsed. Why? First, the successor would begin by "looking at market data." All innovative proposals had to undergo rounds of research, PowerPoint presentations, and committee reviews. As a result, Sony missed almost every wave of opportunity in the digital age: in the MP3 era, it lost to Apple; in the smartphone era, it lost to the iPhone and Samsung; and in the streaming era, it almost completely missed out. Coupled with internal strife within departments, Sony's market capitalization plummeted from its peak of nearly $150 billion in the 1990s to approximately $10 billion in 2012, almost leading to its complete sale. Some might argue that if the company fully respected the founder's vision and thoroughly implemented his style, wouldn't it have maintained its momentum? Not necessarily. For example, the most typical example is Disney. In December 1966, Walt Disney, 65, suddenly died in Los Angeles due to complications from lung cancer surgery. At the time, the Disney Company was at its peak. Disneyland in California had been open for ten years and was doing very well; a new park in Florida was in the process of selecting a site and buying land. All these projects were in the works, and the core leader was suddenly gone. Walt's brother Roy succeeded him, who was 73 years old at the time and already semi-retired. He almost completely followed Walt's approach, even naming the new theme park "Walt Disney World." Roy's role was to continue Walt's work. For the first few years, this strategy worked very well. However, as time went on, the side effects began to appear. There was a habit within the company at the time: whenever a problem arose, people would ask, "If Walt were still here, what would he do?" But it's important to understand that Walt wasn't an omniscient prophet; he couldn't accurately predict future market trends. Thus, this statement, once a methodology, slowly became a constraint. Animators dared not express their own style, and all creative meetings devolved into questions like, "Would Walt agree if he were here?" As a result, for over a decade, Disney only produced mediocre, critically panned films like *Robin Hood* and *The Fox and the Hound*, never again producing a phenomenon like *Snow White* or *Bambi*. By 1984, the company's stock price was depressed, and it nearly faced a hostile takeover. It wasn't until Michael Eisner was brought in as CEO and produced *The Little Mermaid* and *The Lion King* that the company truly emerged from its slump. For Disney, the phrase "What would Walt do?" might seem like a quick fix, but if its implementation is too rigid, it could become a constraint on future innovation. Of course, founders leave companies in countless ways, and each company operates in a different industry, so generalizations cannot be made. For example, McDonald's once changed two CEOs within a year, but it had almost no impact on its performance. This is because McDonald's belongs to the relatively stable catering industry; franchisees and customers don't really care who the CEO is. For example, after Uber's founder Travis Kalanick was forced to resign in 2017, the company's performance actually improved significantly. This was mainly because the founder had too many scandals, and his departure was almost universally expected. After the new CEO took office, he directly and publicly admitted, "Our previous culture was toxic," and then apologized and made necessary changes. However, from the experiences of these different companies, we can still see some commonalities. Whether a company can maintain growth after the founder leaves depends on two key factors. First, is the industry it operates in a rapidly changing one, so fast that there's no time for leisurely meetings and discussions, and many decisions must rely on the founder's intuition? Second, are its customer relationships, company culture, and operating model highly dependent on the founder? Many of these factors are largely determined in the early stages of the company's establishment, not just appearing the moment the founder leaves. How do truly capable people deal with their own resentment? Okay, now that we've talked about the company, let's look at what happened to the founders who left their companies. You'll find that the paths these elites took weren't as "rational" as we imagined; they were all driven by personal emotions to varying degrees. For example, many people would choose "revenge." The most typical example is Zenefits, a human resources management software company that reached a peak valuation of $4.5 billion, making it one of the fastest-growing unicorn companies in Silicon Valley at the time. In February 2016, the company's founder, Parker Conrad, was ousted by the board of directors. The reason was that "the salesperson was involved in using forged certificates." On the day Parker left, the company's investor told him, "You'll never have another company in your life." Later, Parker remembered this sentence vividly and repeated it on many occasions. Less than a year after leaving the company, Parker founded a new one called Rippling, doing the exact same business as his former company, directly competing with it. By 2025, Rippling's valuation reached $16.8 billion, 3.7 times that of Zenefits at its peak. Parker himself later said that half of the reason he did this was for "revenge." Of course, the first thing Parker did when he founded the new company was to establish the ironclad rule of "compliance first". You see, he retained the rational thinking of "a fall into a pit, a gain in your wit," but was also swayed by the emotion of "I want revenge." He used revenge to ignite his entrepreneurial passion, but handed the steering wheel to reason. There are many others whose experiences are full of drama. For example, John Sculley. In 1983, he was poached by Steve Jobs from Pepsi to become Apple's CEO. Jobs' famous quote, "Do you want to sell sugared water for the rest of your life, or do you want to come with me and change the world?" was directed at him. In 1985, he joined forces with the Apple board to oust Jobs from Apple. Then, in 1993, at the age of 54, Sculley himself was ousted from Apple. The reason was poor performance. His life afterwards basically boiled down to one sentence: He spent his whole life trying to prove, "I am also a great CEO," but ended up repeatedly involved in a series of short-lived companies and never made a name for himself again. Among the many founders who left their companies, quite a few left behind very positive methodologies. For example, the famous financier Sandy Weill lost a power struggle at American Express in 1985 and was ousted from the company. Afterwards, instead of fading into obscurity, he spearheaded several successful mergers and acquisitions. In a later interview, when asked about this experience, Sandy Weill said that the most important year of his life was not the year he founded the company, but the year he was ousted. This experience made him reflect on what he personally had left after leaving the company. For example, Jack Dorsey, the founder of Twitter, was fired as CEO by Twitter's board of directors in 2008 at the age of 31, citing "mismanagement." That same day, when he returned to his office, he discovered that his access card was no longer valid. Just four months after leaving Nvidia, Dorsey founded Square, which is today's Block. This company's market capitalization once surpassed Twitter's. Dorsey later said, "Those four months after I was ousted were the four months I've tried to understand the most in my life." There are many more stories like this, and they are incredibly diverse, many more bizarre than any movie. From this perspective, what will happen to Jensen Huang after leaving Nvidia? This question is almost impossible to answer definitively. Some might compare Huang Renxun to Jobs, arguing that both were leading figures in their respective industries. However, others point out that Jobs was only in his early 30s when he was ousted from Apple, while Huang Renxun is 62 this year, 10 years older than Sandy Weir when he was ousted from American Express. Furthermore, the chip industry has extremely high barriers to entry. Taking all these factors into account, the possibility of Huang Renxun "making a comeback" is not high. Although Huang Renxun's future is uncertain, we can still see a common thread in these stories. This is their behavioral pattern. All the names mentioned today are adults who have weathered many storms. However, you'll find that even the most experienced person cannot remain absolutely rational when faced with major upheavals; they too experience pain and resentment. But truly capable individuals use these emotions as a source of motivation, not as a steering wheel. When it comes to crucial decisions, they always return to rationality.
